signals.headline: Trump loyalist Todd Blanche confirmed by Senate as US attorney general
signals.summary: The US senate voted to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general in a major win for Donald Trump, who will now have his one-time personal attorney sitting atop the nation’s law enforcement apparatus.
keyTakeaways: Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana cast the deciding vote in Blanche’s favor after two other Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska – voted against him.
The vote came after Blanche’s nomination had been in limbo for weeks.
That appears to have cost Blanche among at least some GOP senators who will oppose his nomination.
signals.whyItMatters: He faced pushback from Republican senators over the department’s deal to create a $1.8bn so-called “anti-weaponization fund” and to give the president, his sons, and business tax immunity.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So the Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That's right. He was Trump's personal attorney, and now he'll lead the Justice Department.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Was it a close vote?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Close enough. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana cast the deciding vote in his favor.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Did everyone in his party support him?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: No. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski both voted against the nomination.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why the hesitation from some Republicans?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Part of it was timing. The nomination sat in limbo for weeks, and that seems to have cost him support.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Was there a policy concern too?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes. Some senators pushed back on a deal tied to an $1.8bn so-called anti-weaponization fund, and on tax immunity extended to the president, his sons, and their businesses.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So this is being seen as a real win for Trump.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It is. It puts someone close to him directly in charge of federal law enforcement.

ja.headline: トランプ氏の側近ブランシュ氏、米司法長官に就任承認
ja.summary: 米上院は、トッド・ブランシュ氏を司法長官に承認した。トランプ大統領にとって大きな勝利であり、かつての個人弁護士が国の法執行機関の頂点に立つことになる。
keyTakeaways: 共和党のスーザン・コリンズ氏とリサ・マーコウスキー氏が反対票を投じたが、ビル・キャシディ氏が賛成に回り、承認を決定づけた。
指名は数週間にわたり停滞していた。
その停滞が一部の共和党議員の支持離れを招いたとみられる。
ja.whyItMatters: 司法省が総額18億ドル規模の「反武器化基金」を設け、大統領やその息子たち、関連事業に税の免除を与える取り決めを結んだことに、共和党議員から反発が出ていた。

signals.headline: Add to playlist: the anxiety-ridden sugar rush of Tiffany Day and the week’s best new tracks
signals.summary: Enter Tiffany Day, a Wichita-raised artist who first went viral in 2017 when a video of her singing Hallelujah on a school trip blew up online.
keyTakeaways: Only by channeling her frustrations into this year’s anxiety-ridden sugar rush Halo did Day finally regain her early momentum.

After his ultra-emotional, 80s-sampling rap tracks Cry and Southpaw this year, the UK vocalist switches up to singing for his synthwave-ballad debut for XL, restless and upset in the choppy wake of a breakup.
She spent the subsequent years unsuccessfully chipping away at building on that virality, cycling through acoustic guitar covers and bedroom R&B.
signals.whyItMatters: Right now popstar breakthrough and burnout are a hair’s breadth from one another.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So who is Tiffany Day, exactly?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: She's an artist from Wichita who first went viral back in 2017, singing Hallelujah on a school trip.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: That's a big moment. Did it launch her career right away?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Not quite. She spent the following years trying to build on it, moving through acoustic covers and bedroom R&B without quite recapturing that spark.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So what changed this year?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: She channeled her frustrations into a new track called Halo, described as an anxiety-ridden sugar rush. That's what finally brought back her early momentum.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Interesting. Is there another artist in this playlist worth mentioning?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, a UK vocalist who's known for emotional, 80s-sampling rap tracks like Cry and Southpaw. This time he switches to singing, on a synthwave ballad for XL.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What's that song about?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It's restless and upset, written in the choppy aftermath of a breakup.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: It sounds like these artists are all navigating something fragile.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: That's really the theme here. Right now, breakthrough and burnout are only a hair's breadth apart.

ja.headline: 今週の新曲、不安と甘さが入り混じるティファニー・デイ
ja.summary: ウィチタ出身のティファニー・デイは、学校の旅行中に歌った「ハレルヤ」の動画が拡散し、2017年に一躍注目を集めたアーティストだ。
keyTakeaways: 苛立ちを今年の新曲、不安げで甘さの弾けるHaloに注ぎ込んだことで、デイはようやくデビュー当初の勢いを取り戻した。
今年発表した80年代サウンドを取り込んだ感情的なラップ曲「クライ」「サウスポー」を経て、この英国出身の歌手はXLからのシンセウェイブ調バラードのデビュー作で歌唱へと転じる。破局の余韻の中、そこには落ち着かない痛みがにじむ。
その後の数年間、デイはあの話題性の上に何かを築こうと試みたが実らず、アコースティックカバーやベッドルームR&Bを渡り歩いた。
ja.whyItMatters: 今、ポップスターとしての飛躍と燃え尽きは、ほんの一歩の距離にある。

signals.headline: Bluster and backdown have turned Iran war into Trump’s own Groundhog Day
signals.summary: Being the subject of mockery may be the most intense of all Donald Trump’s known aversions.
keyTakeaways: Critics suggest the ultimatum-climbdown sequence has acquired a Groundhog Day quality.

Despite negotiations between Iran and Oman over shipping in the strait of Hormuz, no deal has thus far materialized, and the strategically vital waterway – conduit to a fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war – remains closed.
The US president has also claimed multiple times that the US has “virtually” won the war and that Iran’s regime was clamoring for a deal.
signals.whyItMatters: Last weekend saw the latest episode, as Trump told reporters onboard Air Force One that he had suddenly called off “a massive” attack that he said would have been “the biggest since world war two” after an appeal from US allies and because “I think there’s a deal”.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So what actually happened this time?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Trump said he called off a massive planned attack, one he described as the biggest since World War Two.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why did he pull back?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He says US allies appealed to him, and that he believes there's a deal coming.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is that pattern familiar?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Critics say yes — this ultimatum, then backdown, has a Groundhog Day feel to it now.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What about the strait of Hormuz? I know that matters for oil.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It's still closed. Iran and Oman have been talking, but no deal has come through yet.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: And Trump's take on the war itself?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: He's said several times the US has virtually won, and that Iran's regime is eager for a deal.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: But nothing's actually settled.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Not yet. The waterway that carries a fifth of the world's oil remains shut for now.

ja.headline: 強気と撤回の繰り返し、イラン戦争は堂々巡りに
ja.summary: 嘲笑の対象になることこそ、トランプ氏が最も嫌うことなのかもしれない。
keyTakeaways: 最後通告と撤回の応酬は、まるで同じ一日を繰り返すかのような様相を呈していると批評家は指摘する。
イランとオマーンはホルムズ海峡の航行を巡り交渉を続けているが、合意は依然として成立せず、開戦前は世界の原油供給の五分の一を担っていたこの戦略的要衝は封鎖されたままだ。
トランプ大統領はこれまで幾度も、米国は事実上戦争に勝利し、イラン政権は合意を切望していると主張してきた。
ja.whyItMatters: 先週末にも同様の場面があり、トランプ氏は大統領専用機の機内で記者団に対し、同盟国からの要請と「合意がまとまりそうだ」との判断から、「第二次世界大戦以来最大」になるはずだった大規模攻撃を土壇場で中止したと明かした。

signals.headline: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health
signals.summary: A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media giant’s platforms.
keyTakeaways: At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, and imposed the maximum penalty: a $375m fine.
The ruling on Thursday is an addition to that fine, bringing the total amount Meta is responsible for to $942m.
Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the bulk of the money – $420m – would be used for treatment services for young people in New Mexico.
signals.whyItMatters: Several former Meta moderators told the Guardian there were instances where they flagged harmful content related to child grooming, but the cases were not escalated.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So a court has ordered Meta to pay out over harms to children's mental health?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, a New Mexico court ordered $567m, paid into a fund to address those harms.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is that on top of something else, or is that the whole penalty?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It's an addition. A jury earlier found Meta knowingly harmed children's mental health and hid what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, and fined it $375m.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So together that's...

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Right, $942m in total that Meta is now responsible for.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Where does most of this new money go?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: The judge said $420m of it will fund treatment services for young people in New Mexico.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: That's a heavy topic. Has anything else come up about how these cases were handled internally?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, former Meta moderators told the Guardian they'd flagged content related to child grooming, but some of those cases weren't escalated.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: That's sobering to hear.

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It is. It's part of why this ruling is being watched so closely.

ja.headline: 米ニューメキシコ州、メタに5億6700万ドルの支払い命令 子どもの心の健康被害めぐり
ja.summary: 米ニューメキシコ州の裁判所は、フェイスブックの親会社メタに対し、同社のプラットフォームが子どもの心の健康に与えた被害を償う基金に5億6700万ドルを拠出するよう命じた。
keyTakeaways: 陪審は当時、メタが子どもの心の健康を知りながら害し、プラットフォーム上の児童性的搾取についても把握していた事実を隠していたと認定し、最高額となる3億7500万ドルの制裁金を科していた。
今回の判決はこの制裁金に上乗せされる形で、メタが負う総額は9億4200万ドルに達する。
ブライアン・ビードシャイド判事によれば、このうち大半にあたる4億2000万ドルは、ニューメキシコ州内の若者向け治療サービスに充てられるという。
ja.whyItMatters: 元メタのモデレーター複数人がガーディアン紙に語ったところによれば、児童の性的懐柔に関わる有害コンテンツを通報しても、対応が進まなかった事例があったという。

signals.headline: The White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy
signals.summary: So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies.
keyTakeaways: On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft attended a private meeting with White House officials to review the AI framework.
The White House, OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
In June, the White House issued an executive order that called for AI companies to voluntarily submit their new models for government review up to 30 days before release.
signals.whyItMatters: Discussions over creating an AI cybersecurity framework began earlier this year after the release of Anthropic’s Mythos model, which the company withheld from public release in April over concerns that it could be used to hack into IT and financial systems.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: So what actually happened here?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft met privately with White House officials.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What were they discussing?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: A framework for vetting AI models that might be dangerous, but the details are being kept private.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Why does that matter?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It's a blow to transparency, and it could work in favor of AI companies that prefer to stay secretive.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Did anyone explain the secrecy?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: No. The White House, OpenAI and Anthropic all declined to comment.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: Is there a policy behind this already?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: Yes, in June the White House issued an order asking companies to voluntarily submit new models for review up to 30 days before release.

captions.speaker: listener
captions.text: What sparked all this?

captions.speaker: explainer
captions.text: It traces back to April, when Anthropic withheld its Mythos model over concerns it could be used to hack IT and financial systems.

ja.headline: ホワイトハウスのAI安全審査計画、詳細は非公開
ja.summary: 危険性のあるAIを審査するホワイトハウスの枠組みは、いまだ詳細が明らかにされていない。透明性の後退であると同時に、情報開示に消極的なAI企業にとっては都合の良い状況ともなっている。
keyTakeaways: 火曜日、OpenAI、Anthropic、Meta、Google、Nvidia、Microsoftの担当者がホワイトハウス関係者と非公開会合を開き、AIの枠組みを検討した。
ホワイトハウス、OpenAI、Anthropicはいずれも取材に応じていない。
6月にホワイトハウスが発した大統領令は、新型AIモデルを公開の最長30日前までに政府審査へ任意提出するようAI企業に求めていた。
ja.whyItMatters: AIのサイバーセキュリティ枠組みをめぐる議論は、Anthropicが4月に公開を見送ったモデル「Mythos」がIT・金融システムへの侵入に悪用され得るとの懸念をきっかけに、今年始まった。
